newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook - Mixed week seen, zinc lively.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook - Mixed week seen, zinc lively.

text.p: Base metal markets are set for a mixed week on the London Metal Exchange (LME), with some likely to be high flyers but others expected to struggle, analysts said.
The zinc market broke above $1,400 a tonne late last week to hit levels not seen since October 1990.
Nickel and copper would remain sensitive to developments at the long-running strike at Inco's Sudbury facilities, but aluminium was likely to continue floundering below $1,600.
Market turnovers might not be too large due to several industry events taking place in Europe this week.
"There are conferences in London, Helsinki and Germany, so there will be a lot of people away from their desks. Also, its summer, and physicals are slowing," one analyst said.
In zinc, the current strength was slightly surprising, but typical of a market where funds were involved on the long side.
Analyst Robin Bhar of LME trader Brandeis said the market had become over-extended on the charts and should in theory retrace back to $1,350/60.
However, the fundamentals this year had been positive, with the market heading for a supply/demand deficit while stocks continued to fall, counfounding talk of Chinese deliveries soon.
"Despite all the talk of Chinese zinc, there has not been much evidence of that in LME stocks, although presumably it is only a matter of time before it is put on warrant," Bhar said.
Consumers had been holding back at these high price levels, unwillinging to chase the market higher.
"But if the pull-back does not come they will have to bite the bullet," he said.
In nickel, the outcome of current talks at Inco's Sudbury facilities in Canada would be important, as would power problems at Russia's Norilsk.
Copper traders would continue to prepare for another spell of tightness, with cash/threes at a wide $127 backwardation on Friday.
Tightness was building up in July/August - yet another sign that the copper market remained finely balanced on supply, demand and stocks.
"There are shorts who yet again are having to cover, and the longs are taking advantage,' an anlyst said.
